Recent advances in question-answering models have led to a surge in interest for representing knowledge through factual triples and incorporating them into pre-training protocols. This surge has sparked debate on whether these triple-based models excel over traditional text-based models when tackling question-answering tasks, particularly within closed-domain settings. In an effort to conduct a comprehensive assessment, we created a knowledge graph from a large knowledge base and pre-trained six popular models using either the triple-based or text-based approach on this graph. We then conducted extensive evaluations on 15 question-answering datasets within closed-domain settings, consisting of 12 domain-specific datasets and 3 multi-domain datasets, and also explored the impact of model size, task complexity, and domain adaptation. Our findings reveal that triple-based models generally outperform text-based models, but are not universally superior, and the advantage is largely diminished when increasing the size of the pre-training data. We also observed that the effectiveness of triple-based models is heavily influenced by the quality of pre-trained knowledge and the accuracy of entity recognition in question annotations. Our results demonstrate that pre-trained models with the best performance are not significantly better than the upper bound established by text-based models, and the average industry standard for question-answering models is approximately 20% lower than the theoretical limit. We believe that the potential of triple-based models is constrained by the imprecision in entity recognition and the lack of comprehensive knowledge in the graph, and that further research is necessary to fully harness the potential of these models.

The linear subsystem approach is a method for analyzing complex systems by decomposing them into smaller linear subystems within certain linear subspaces. What makes this method effective is that it allows for the application of linear system theory to address control and estimation problems in a piecewise linear system. However, for fractional order dynamic systems, implementing this approach is complicated due to the need to establish conditions for linear subspaces to be invariant under the system's dynamics. Here, we resolve that issue by determining the invariance of linear subspaces in a class of fractional order dynamic multi-systems by leveraging the underlying linear dynamics within each system component. We also prove that in the fractional order dynamic multi-system, the linear subspaces will be closed under the system's dynamics if the following conditions are met: (1) the subspaces are closed under the underlying linear dynamics in each system component, and (2) there are control inputs available to shift between any two subspaces within the collection of subspaces in question. We demonstrate that in a general fractional order dynamic multi-system, the linear subspaces will be closed under the system's dynamics if and only if the above conditions are met. We also show that the optimal linear feedback control that steers the system within the specified linear subspaces around a given initial state $x_0$ to a target state $r$ in the same subspace is unique. Moreover, we prove that the minimum time required to achieve the target state is linear in the system's dimension, and that the optimal control input that drives the system to the target state within the specified linear subspaces is piecewise linear in the system's output around the initial state $x_0$. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach by applying it to a mass-spring system with inertial constraints and a linear mechanical system with inertial constraints in a two-dimensional plane. We also compare our method to existing approaches by providing a numerical example that demonstrates the method's superiority over those approaches. We anticipate that our results will be useful in applying linear system theory to a wide range of piecewise linear systems, including systems with time-delays, systems with partial state information, and systems with constrained control inputs. We also anticipate that our findings will be beneficial in various applications, including robotics, traffic flow control, and chemical reaction engineering.
